messages.text: how does the alia works

Here's the mechanic, Tilux.

**Every deployment gets its own immutable URL.** When Vercel builds your project, it assigns a unique, long, random-looking address tied to *that exact build*. Yours was:
`tiluxmobile-aahtvtiss-tiluxs-projects.vercel.app`

That URL is locked to that one build forever. Deploy again and you get a *new* random URL - the old one still points to the old snapshot.

**An alias is a stable nickname pointing at a deployment.** That's what the clean URL is:
`tiluxmobileweb.vercel.app` → currently pointing at `tiluxmobile-aahtvtiss-...`

So the alias is just a pointer. It says "whenever someone hits this nice short name, send them to **that** build."

**Why it matters:** the alias stays constant while the messy build URL changes underneath it. So your users always bookmark `tiluxmobileweb.vercel.app`, and you can swap which build it points to behind the scenes without anyone noticing.

**How you reassign one:**
```
vercel alias set <new-deployment-url> tiluxmobileweb.vercel.app
```
That's how you'd flip the stable name over to your next deploy.

**The plumbing I set up for you:** I registered two aliases per project so both work:
- `tiluxmobileweb.vercel.app` (your top-level clean name)
- `tiluxmobileweb-tiluxs-projects.vercel.app` (the team-scoped version)

Confirmed live just now - the alias is returning **HTTP 200**. So the pointer is healthy and serving your build.

Short version: build URL = the actual house, alias = the sign on the door that you can re-point anytime.

messages.text:
Can customize ai mouse that can click ok anything work on wayland?
Just asking

Short answer: yes, Tilux - but not with the tools you'd normally reach for. Wayland blocks those on purpose.

**Why the usual route dies:** Wayland's whole security model is that no random client gets to move your cursor or inject clicks globally - otherwise any app could take over your desktop. So:
- `xdotool` → **dead.** It's X11-only.
- `pyautogui` → **crippled.** It works only inside XWayland windows, and can't move the real cursor or click arbitrary spots.

**What actually works on Wayland:**
- **`ydotool` / `dotool`** → the real answer. They inject at the **kernel level** via `uinput`, so the compositor sees them as a physical mouse. Compositor-agnostic, works on GNOME, KDE, Sway, Hyprland. Needs root or membership in the `input`/`uinput` group, plus a `ydotoold` daemon running.
- **`wtype`** → keyboard injection only, via the virtual-keyboard protocol.
- **`grim`** (wlroots) or the **XDG Desktop Portal** screenshot API → how you grab the screen for OCR. Portals may pop a one-time permission prompt.
- **`tesseract`** → OCR itself is unaffected. No restrictions.

**So the "AI mouse that clicks anything" pipeline looks like:**
1. Portal/grim screenshot
2. Tesseract OCR → gives you text *and* its bounding box
3. Convert box → absolute screen coordinates
4. `ydotool mousemove` + `ydotool click`

**Caveats to know up front:**
- Coordinate math breaks under fractional scaling/DPI — offsets get ugly.
- A few native Wayland apps and games ignore synthetic input entirely.
- The daemon needs boot-level `uinput` access — a systemd user service.
- Portals can show a consent prompt the first time.

This is genuinely the upgrade path for your setup — right now my automation uses pyautogui/xdotool, which is exactly why I have to fall back to keyboard shortcuts instead of real clicking. Swap in `ydotool`, and I could click reliably on Wayland.

Not touching anything — you asked. Want me to set it up when you're ready?
